title: Federal Plan Forces Deep Water Cuts on Arizona, California, and Nevada as Colorado River Reservoirs Hit Record Lows
excerpt: A new two-year Interior Department plan mandates a 27% cut to Arizona, 10% to California, and 16% to Nevada through 2028, with no mandatory reductions for upper basin states.
body:
• The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation published a two-year operating plan on Friday mandating deep water cuts from the Colorado River for Arizona (760,000 acre-feet), California (440,000 acre-feet), and Nevada (50,000 acre-feet) through 2028.
  • The cuts amount to roughly a 27% reduction for Arizona, 10% for California, and 16% for Nevada — with no mandatory reductions for the four upper basin states.
  • Lake Mead and Lake Powell have both fallen to record lows, threatening water and hydroelectric power for tens of millions of people across the West.
  • Arizona officials warn the cuts could shut off the Central Arizona Project canal entirely, devastating water supplies for the Phoenix and Tucson metro areas where a combined 6 million people live.

The Federal Intervention

The Department of the Interior published a new two-year operating plan on Friday stipulating exactly how much water Arizona, California, and Nevada must give up from the Colorado River through 2028 — the first concrete enforcement step under a broader 10-year framework the Bureau of Reclamation released in July.

Arizona will endure the steepest cuts at 760,000 acre-feet, California will lose 440,000 acre-feet, and Nevada will take a reduction of 50,000 acre-feet. The plan sets out no mandatory cuts for the upper basin states of Utah, Colorado, Wyoming, and New Mexico.

Those numbers translate to roughly a 27% cut for Arizona, 10% for California, and 16% for Nevada, according to Sarah Porter, director of the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University. For Arizona water users specifically, the reduction amounts to a 50% cut, she said.

"I would like the reductions for Arizona to be zero but that's not the reality we're facing. It's a pretty good outcome."

— Tom Buschatzke, Director, Arizona Department of Water Resources

Record-Low Reservoirs

The plan arrives at a moment of genuine crisis. Lake Mead, the country's largest reservoir, has dropped to its lowest level since it was created nine decades ago. Lake Powell reached a record low on August 15. Together, the two reservoirs are near the point where their hydroelectric power plants stop functioning.

The Colorado River provides water to around 40 million people and irrigates more than 5 million acres of farmland across seven states. After the smallest winter snowpack on record, the Bureau of Reclamation said the reservoirs are at their lowest combined levels since 1957.

Climate change models project an additional 20% decline in Colorado River flow by 2050 and 35% by 2100. A 2022 UCLA study found the U.S. West is in its worst drought in at least 1,200 years.

Why It Came to This

The seven basin states — Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming, Arizona, California, and Nevada — spent more than three years trying to negotiate how to share the shrinking river. They missed multiple federal deadlines, including one in February and another last November. When they failed to reach a consensus, the Bureau of Reclamation stepped in with its own plan.

The lower basin states had proposed a 21% reduction in their combined supplies through 2028, totaling about 1.6 million acre-feet per year. The federal framework envisages cuts of up to 3 million acre-feet — nearly twice what the states offered.

Upper basin states have resisted cuts, arguing that decades of drought have already slashed the water available to them and that the lower basin — which uses far more water to support sprawling farms and fast-growing cities — should shoulder the reductions.

Arizona Braces for Impact

Under the river's century-old priority system, the earlier a town or irrigator started using Colorado River water, the higher their priority during shortages. The Central Arizona Project canal, authorized in 1968, holds relatively junior water rights. If lower basin cuts approach 40%, the canal would lose all of its water before a single drop is cut from California users with far older rights, Arizona officials have warned.

The Phoenix and Tucson metropolitan areas, with a combined population of nearly 6 million, rely heavily on the canal for their water supply. Arizona's Democratic Senators Ruben Gallego and Mark Kelly issued a joint statement supporting the new guidelines, but the state's earlier reaction to the July framework was sharply critical — the Arizona Department of Water Resources called the proposed reductions "unacceptable" and said they "would devastate Arizona's water users and its economy."

"We are at a time of tremendous change in how we are managing water in this system and what that means for both communities and the river itself."

— Celene Hawkins, Director, Colorado River Program, The Nature Conservancy

Litigation Looms

Water scientist Sharon Megdal called the river's condition a "natural disaster" requiring extraordinary action to sustain livelihoods in a region that supports an estimated $1.4 trillion in GDP and 16 million jobs.

Experts fear the dispute will end up in court. States could sue each other or the federal government, and Arizona has previously signaled it may pursue a legal route. Any lawsuit would likely take years to resolve — years during which the Colorado River looks set to keep declining.

The seven states can continue negotiating a voluntary agreement that would supersede the federal plan. But experts are not confident a deal is coming soon. Metropolitan Water District of Southern California General Manager Shivaji Deshmukh warned that "water users across the Basin must make a renewed effort to forge a longer-term agreement that produces additional reductions, including through participation of all seven Basin states."

What It Means for Western Communities

The Colorado River cuts will ripple through communities across the Southwest, including major metro areas with significant Indian diaspora populations. Phoenix, Tucson, Las Vegas, and Southern California all depend on the river, and rising water costs and potential supply disruptions could affect millions of residents. The cuts will be reassessed every two years, meaning prolonged uncertainty for homeowners, farmers, and businesses across the region.
